title: Currency of the Thirteen Colonies
summary: Paper money in the American colonies began in Massachusetts in 1690. Unable to pay returning soldiers in coin, the colony issued paper notes instead—the first government paper money in the Western world.
introduction: Other colonies followed. Coin remained chronically scarce, and colonial legislatures began issuing their own bills of credit to meet local needs. By the eve of independence, each of the thirteen colonies had developed its own paper currency, with its own designs, denominations, rules, and experiments in how money should work. This exhibition brings those currencies together through one representative note from each colony.

curatorialLens.label: A collection shaped by its gaps
curatorialLens.description: The thirteen colonies provide the framework, but the objects resist a tidy national story: dates cross the Revolution, denominations differ, and one New Jersey example is itself a contemporary counterfeit.

artifacts.title: 1754 40s North Carolina Forty Shillings
artifacts.description: Dated 1754, this forty-shilling note anchors North Carolina within the collecting map. Its survival makes the colony tangible through an object designed to circulate, be handled, and eventually disappear.
artifacts.subtitle: An early anchor for the southern colonies
researchNotes: This is currently the earliest dated object in the thirteen-colony sequence.
Future research can add the printer, issue authorization, signers, and precise catalog attribution.

artifacts.title: 1763 12s New Jersey Colonial Note - Contemporary Counterfeit
artifacts.description: This contemporary counterfeit twelve-shilling note complicates the idea of a representative colonial issue. It belongs on the map because imitation was part of the monetary world: trust, recognition, and deception traveled with paper currency.

images.alt: 1763 12s New Jersey Colonial Note - Contemporary Counterfeit, photograph 1
1763 12s New Jersey Colonial Note - Contemporary Counterfeit, photograph 2

artifacts.subtitle: A representative object that was never legitimate
researchNotes: Recorded as Fr. NJ-156CT and identified in the collection as a contemporary counterfeit.
Its presence keeps the exhibition from equating representative with officially authorized.

artifacts.title: 1774 $4 Maryland Colonial Currency
artifacts.description: Maryland's four-dollar note was dated April 10, 1774 and printed by Anne Catherine and Frederick Green. On the map it sits close to neighboring issues, while its denomination and printed identity remain distinctly local.
artifacts.subtitle: Printed on the eve of political rupture
researchNotes: The collection record identifies the note as Fr. MD-68, serial number 14042.
Printer attribution comes from the existing ArchiveSense collection record.

artifacts.title: 1777 £4 Pennsylvania Colonial Currency
artifacts.description: Dated April 10, 1777, this Pennsylvania four-pound note was issued after independence had been declared. Its place in the exhibition is deliberately transitional: the former colony remained a geographic collecting category even as its political identity changed.
artifacts.subtitle: A colonial collecting framework crossing into revolution
researchNotes: The collection record identifies the note as PA-224a, serial number 10507, with Eric P. Newman Collection provenance.
The thirteen-colony map is a collecting framework, not a claim that every represented object predates independence.

artifacts.title: 1780 10 s Connecticut Colonial Note
artifacts.description: Connecticut's ten-shilling note, dated July 1, 1780, extends the sequence into the Revolutionary era. It marks Connecticut's place while also showing why a geographic collection cannot be confined to a single political moment.
artifacts.subtitle: A former colony issuing money during the Revolution
researchNotes: The collection record identifies the note as Fr. CT-238, serial number 3063.
Only one Connecticut object is pinned to the map so the exhibition can retain its one-sample-per-colony discipline.

artifacts.title: Banque Royale January 1, 1720. 10 Livres
artifacts.description: This Banque Royale ten-livres note, associated in the collection record with France and Louisiana, sits outside the thirteen-colony checklist. It remains in view as a reminder that colonial North American money was never bounded by the later United States.
artifacts.subtitle: A wider colonial monetary world
researchNotes: The collection record identifies the note as P-A16b and records a PMG grade of Very Fine 30.
It is presented beside, rather than inside, the thirteen-colony map.
